entriesApplied.topic: Muscadet: Melon alone only in the three named zones
entriesApplied.claim: The Loire record calls Melon de Bourgogne Muscadet's only grape and says Muscadet is Melon de Bourgogne alone, and the Régionale question i-r0p7056l says Melon has been the sole grape of Muscadet ever since the winter of 1709.
entriesApplied.finding: The specification of the plain Muscadet AOC names Melon B as principal grape and Chardonnay B as an accessory grape, at no more than 10 per cent of a holding's plantings. INAO's standing committee took up the change in 2017, it went to national opposition in November 2018, it stands in the specification homologated by the arrêté of 5 February 2021 (amended 27 May 2021), and the arrêté of 26 November 2025 (JORF of 3 December 2025) keeps it. Muscadet Sèvre et Maine, Muscadet Coteaux de la Loire and Muscadet Côtes de Grandlieu remain Melon B alone. The history in the question stands: the specification's link to origin says the hard winter of 1709 destroyed most of the Nantes vineyard and Melon, which bears frost better, was replanted, and InterLoire says the same.
entriesApplied.why: The plain appellation has admitted an accessory Chardonnay since its specification was revised, so only the three named zones are Melon alone; the 1709 story is the rule's own and stays.
entriesApplied.refuterNote: Searched for a stricter or newer text: the regional Muscadet rule names melon B as principal and chardonnay B as accessory at no more than 10 per cent of the holding's plantings, in the specification of 2021 and in the version adopted by the national committee on 12 June 2025; the named zones' texts (Coteaux de la Loire, Cotes de Grandlieu) read melon B alone, and a secondary page reads the same for all three. A 2024 committee paper speaks of a request to lift the accessory share to 20 per cent for a time; whether it was granted was not found, and the new texts give no figure, so they hold either way. The three old strings occur once each, in the Loire record's Melon row, r-hksiq6zd's explanation and i-r0p7056l's explanation in r1_loire.py; the stem, answer and options of both questions stay right (Melon de Bourgogne). One correction: i-r0p7056l's new text named Sevre et Maine alone, which leaves a reader to wonder about Coteaux de la Loire and Cotes de Grandlieu; it now says the other two named zones, the phrase the same bank uses in its Sevre et Maine question. ASCII kept, as r1_loire.py is. Completeness: no other line in js/, the region fragments, the CMS banks, rewrite/categories or the grape fragments calls Melon Muscadet's only or sole grape (the Melon grape fragment already says the rule loosened; MASTER m-zf6jp55w says replanted almost to the exclusion of everything else, true of 1709). The CP127 dossier and the Legifrance id were not opened from here.

entriesApplied.topic: Melon came to Nantes before 1709
entriesApplied.claim: The CMS Loire question e-ddtr2ora says the Melon variety came from Burgundy after the hard winter of 1709.
entriesApplied.finding: Melon was already in the Pays Nantais before 1709: the Muscadet specification puts the first written traces of plantings under the name Muscadet in the middle of the seventeenth century (a lease of 1635 kept at Gorges), and after the winter of 1709 Melon was replanted across the vineyard. The frost made it the grape of the region; it did not bring it.
entriesApplied.why: The frost of 1709 spread the grape across the Pays Nantais; the grape itself was there before it, so the explanation should not date its arrival to 1709.
entriesApplied.refuterNote: Tested whether Melon arrived only after 1709. Search summaries of the Muscadet Sevre et Maine specification put the first written record of the Burgundian plant under the name Muscadet in the middle of the seventeenth century (a lease of 1635 at Gorges) and say melon B was established in the Nantes vineyard well before the frost; one secondary source puts Melon at Nantes as early as 1616. All agree the winter of 1709 is what made it the grape of the whole vineyard. So came from Burgundy after the hard winter of 1709 misdates the arrival, and the new text (came from Burgundy and took over the Pays Nantais after it) is right. The old string occurs once, in e-ddtr2ora's explanation; the answer Melon B and the other three rationales stay true. The stem of i-r0p7056l (growers replanted with a Burgundian white) speaks of the replanting, not the arrival, and L1-10 rightly leaves it. No other place dates the arrival to 1709.

entriesApplied.topic: Rueda: one white category since 2019, the main grapes at 75 per cent since 2024
entriesApplied.claim: The Rueda and Toro record teaches Rueda Verdejo and Rueda Sauvignon as label categories at 85 per cent of their grape and plain Rueda as at least 50 per cent Verdejo, with Viura merely permitted in that blend; the Spain module question c-lalvjliu and the Verdejo grape fragment repeat the half.
entriesApplied.finding: The Consejo Regulador merged Rueda Verdejo, Rueda Sauvignon and Rueda into one white category, Rueda, from the 2019 vintage; the amended pliego (published nationally on 29 October 2019, in force at EU level from 3 March 2020) asked at least 50 per cent of the main whites, then Verdejo and Sauvignon Blanc, and admitted Chardonnay and Viognier as secondary. From 30 August 2024 (BOCYL of that day; EU communication of 12 June 2025) a Rueda white needs at least 75 per cent from the main whites, now Verdejo, Sauvignon Blanc, Viura, Chardonnay and Viognier, and may be all of them. A grape named on the label must still make at least 85 per cent, by EU rule. Plain Rueda therefore has no Verdejo floor of its own. The wines notes for Rueda Verdejo and Rueda Sauvignon and the Verdejo label line say at least 85 per cent of a named grape, which is still true, and are left.
entriesApplied.why: Two revisions of the pliego (2019 to 2020 and August 2024) replaced the varietal categories and the half Verdejo rule; the stem of r-zd9qzdui now has two right options, Sauvignon Blanc and Chardonnay, so it is reworded to the old category and keeps its pinned id, its answer, options and accept list.
entriesApplied.refuterNote: Tried to refute on four points. One: the merge of the varietal categories from the 2019 vintage stands on the council's note of November 2019 and on the ministry's text of the request (Sauvignon Blanc made a main variety, Chardonnay and Viognier admitted as secondary, Gran Vino de Rueda new). Two: the August 2024 change stands on the council's own press note (75 per cent main, at most 25 secondary, a wine may be all main varieties; Viura, Viognier and Chardonnay made main) and on the EU notice C/2025/3217 (from at least 50 to at least 75 per cent). Three: Palomino is still permitted, as a secondary white, on the council's variety page and in the Decanter report it hosts, so the new texts may name it in the remainder; Godello's entry as a secondary was suspended on 28 October 2024 and no new text names it. Four: the stem of r-zd9qzdui is wrong today, since Chardonnay, now a main white, may be named at 85 per cent beside Sauvignon Blanc, while Garnacha Blanca and Godello, secondary, cannot reach 85 per cent under the 75 per cent rule; the reworded stem has one right option, Sauvignon Blanc, and its id stays pinned. Corrections to the new texts: a share of three quarters is a floor, so r-99qkjr18, c-lalvjliu and the Verdejo grape question now say at least three quarters; the remainder may be any permitted white, main ones included, so the texts that said the rest from Palomino or the balance from the other whites now say the rest open to, may take or may make up; the trap's elided verb is restored (has no set share). Every old string occurs once in its file and sits in the record and path named. r-99qkjr18 still answers 85 per cent (its 75 per cent option is now explained by the text rather than made right by it), c-lalvjliu still answers at least eighty five per cent, and the Verdejo grape question still answers at least 85 per cent. Completeness: no other place in js/, the fragments, the CMS banks or rewrite/categories states the half Verdejo rule; the 85 per cent lines L1-09 leaves are true of a label naming the grape. r-99qkjr18 is held to the 60 word cap of a region question (60 words, at the cap; check-fragment passes on a copy with every spain.1 edit applied).

entriesApplied.topic: Verdejo and Verdelho: a different grape, not unrelated
entriesApplied.claim: The Rueda trap says Verdejo is not Verdelho and that the Madeira grape is unrelated.
entriesApplied.finding: They are different varieties, but not shown unrelated: the institutes' catalogue makes Verdejo a probable cross of Savagnin and Castellana Blanca on genetic analyses at Montpellier, and a DNA study of 2018 makes Verdelho an offspring of Savagnin with an unknown other parent, which would make the two half siblings. Both results rest on small marker sets, so the safe wording is a different grape, as the Verdejo and Godello grape fragments already say.
entriesApplied.why: Unrelated says more than the DNA allows; a different grape is true on every reading.
entriesApplied.refuterNote: Looked for proof that the two are unrelated and found the reverse: the catalogue of the French institutes gives Verdejo as a probable Savagnin and Castellana Blanca cross, and two independent pages give Verdelho as an offspring of Savagnin (one a glossary on DNA of 2018, one a wine reference that lists Verdelho among Savagnin's close relations). Both rest on few markers, so a different grape is the claim true on every reading. The old string occurs once, in the Rueda record's traps[0]; it sits beside nothing it would contradict. Completeness: the Godello and Verdejo grape fragments already read a different grape; no other record calls Verdelho unrelated to Verdejo (L1-06 takes the one other unrelated, in i-fw8igegc).

entriesApplied.topic: Trebbiano d'Abruzzo: the vines the rule names
entriesApplied.claim: Question c-ndvwbnke says the denomination permits Bombino Bianco as well as Trebbiano Abruzzese; the Italy country record says Trebbiano d'Abruzzo is a different grape from Trebbiano Toscano, while the Abruzzo record says the wine may be made from Trebbiano Abruzzese and Trebbiano Toscano, at least 85 per cent together.
entriesApplied.finding: The rule of 1972 named Trebbiano d'Abruzzo with Bombino Bianco, the two long confused in the vineyard. The disciplinare approved by ministerial decree of 19 January 2023 (Gazzetta Ufficiale of 6 February 2023) names Trebbiano Abruzzese and/or Trebbiano Toscano, at least 85 per cent, and no longer Bombino Bianco; the region's comparison of texts of December 2024 says Article 2 no longer provides for Bombino, and reports of the ordinary amendment approved in August 2026 give the same base. Trebbiano Abruzzese the vine is distinct from Trebbiano Toscano; the wine Trebbiano d'Abruzzo may be made from either.
entriesApplied.why: The explanation gave the pre 2023 rule as current and two lines called the wine a grape; c-ndvwbnke's stem, answer and accept list stay (Bombino Bianco is still what old vineyards planted as Trebbiano often hold, and the accept list takes Trebbiano Abruzzese).
entriesApplied.refuterNote: The base of the rule holds: the region's own bulletin of December 2024 sets out the text in force, the disciplinare as amended by the decree of 19 January 2023 (G.U. no. 30 of 6 February 2023), and it reads Trebbiano Abruzzese and/or Trebbiano Toscano at least 85 per cent, the sub-zones 90; Federdoc's listing of 2020 still read Trebbiano Abruzzese and/or Bombino Bianco and/or Trebbiano Toscano. So Bombino left the named base between 2020 and the 2023 text, but nothing read shows the 2023 decree itself made that cut, and the search summaries did not show the bulletin's own words on Bombino that the finding quotes. The new explanation of c-ndvwbnke therefore says the rule as amended in January 2023 names the two Trebbianos (true whichever decree dropped Bombino) in place of since January 2023. Its stem, answer and accept list stay true: the stem speaks of what reaches the bottle, the explanation keeps the vineyard confusion that puts Bombino Bianco there, and the accept list takes Trebbiano Abruzzese. country.grapes[10].styles: may use either read loosely and now reads may be made from either. The other three targets read well in place; the r1 Ugni Blanc question still answers a single vine, and the Verdicchio page's question still answers Verdicchio di Matelica. Every old string occurs once in its file. Completeness: the Abruzzo record's tier, trap and card, the Trebbiano page's home line, label row and card already give Abruzzese and Toscano at 85 per cent; no other place says the DOC permits Bombino Bianco, and the Puglia record's Bombino Bianco row makes no Abruzzo claim. bura.regione.abruzzo.it and www.vinidabruzzo.it refused a fetch, so both were read by search summary.

entriesApplied.topic: Turbiana and Verdicchio
entriesApplied.claim: The Lombardy, Marche and Italy records, two questions, a producer note and the Trebbiano and Verdicchio grape pages say Lugana's Turbiana (once Trebbiano di Lugana) is Verdicchio, the same vine as Trebbiano di Soave.
entriesApplied.finding: For Trebbiano di Soave every source agrees it is Verdicchio. For Turbiana the studies differ: the Vitis study of 2001 found Trebbiano di Soave identical to Verdicchio and Trebbiano di Lugana very similar; a study in Advances in Horticultural Science (2012) found one DNA profile across 25 accessions, a Turbiana among them; the Lugana consortium treats Turbiana as a distinct vine closely related to Verdicchio, which is why Lugana took the name. So Turbiana is so close to Verdicchio that it is often taught as the same vine, but not proven identical.
entriesApplied.why: Only the Turbiana half was overstated: Trebbiano di Soave stays Verdicchio everywhere (the Veneto record and friuli's r-ls1a2rd8 are right), the accept list of r-uf2jj6ug keeps Verdicchio, the Marche styles line already says DNA ties it and stays, and the Verdicchio page's aliases and regions list keep Turbiana by the grape plan.
entriesApplied.refuterNote: Tried to refute the softening from both sides. Towards identity: the national register files Turbiana and Trebbiano di Lugana as synonyms of Trebbiano di Soave, itself filed under Verdicchio Bianco, and the 2012 study found one profile across 25 accessions, a Turbiana among them. Towards a separate vine: the consortium has held since its announcement of 2021 that Turbiana is a distinct vine closely related to Verdicchio, has registered Turbiana clones of its own, and two trade reports call it a biotype. Identity is unproven either way, so so close to Verdicchio in DNA studies that it is often taught as the same vine, and tied by DNA, are true on every reading; Trebbiano di Soave stays Verdicchio. Paths: three targets in trebbiano.json named the wrong index; the strings sit at labels[4].means, compare[1].tell and cards[1].back, now corrected. profile.confuse: Lugana's its near twin read as a fragment and now reads Trebbiano di Soave is Verdicchio, Lugana's Turbiana nearly so, which keeps the line at the page's cap of 30 words. Every old string occurs once in its file. Answers stay true: r-uf2jj6ug answers Turbiana and may keep Verdicchio in its accept list while the register files the names as one vine; c-7zyl7br8 answers Turbiana; c-lhywvj93 answers Trebbiano di Soave. Left for the owner: the Verdicchio page's questions[1] stem asks for a wine of the same grape as a Lugana; not shown wrong while the register treats them as one, so it stays. Completeness: a grep of js/, the region fragments, the CMS, the rewrite banks and the grape pages finds no further place that states Turbiana is Verdicchio; the Marche styles line, the Verdicchio page's label row, guest answer and profile, and friuli's r-ls1a2rd8 already say tied, as near as makes no difference, or Lugana's grape; the Trebbiano page's notIn line sits in its report, which never ships.

entriesApplied.topic: Sicily: the 2017 rule and Grillo's billing
entriesApplied.claim: The Sicily record says in six places that varietal Nero d'Avola and Grillo must be Sicilia DOC since 2017, while its card cards[6] and question r-ih3gzpr1 say the names belong to the island's DOCs, Sicilia above all; three lines call Grillo the island's best dry or varietal white.
entriesApplied.finding: The change in force from the 2017 harvest amended the Terre Siciliane IGT rule: Grillo and Calabrese (Nero d'Avola) may no longer be named on an IGT label, in varietal or optional information. It reserves nothing to Sicilia DOC alone: the island's other DOCs still name the grapes, Noto DOC for one keeps a Noto Nero d'Avola of at least 85 per cent, and Eloro and Vittoria name it too. A challenge before the regional administrative court was overturned by the Council of State, which upheld the change. Calling Grillo the island's best white is a judgement the house rules keep out.
entriesApplied.why: The rule bars the IGT and admits every Sicilian DOC, as cards[6] and r-ih3gzpr1 already say; the CMS question's stem (unless a smaller DOC applies) and answer stay, only its explanation moves. Best is a superlative of judgement and is cut.
entriesApplied.refuterNote: The rule holds as the entry gives it: the amended Terre Siciliane text bars IGT Grillo and Nero d'Avola from the 2017 vintage, the Council of State upheld it, and the consortium's director said the two belong to every Sicilian DOC that names them, not to Sicilia alone; the trade reports of 2017 agree. Two new texts named Noto and Vittoria as DOCs for both grapes, but those name Nero d'Avola and no Grillo type was found in either; Erice DOC has a Grillo type of its own. traps[7] and the CMS explanation now name Erice for Grillo and Noto for Nero d'Avola. Nothing else moves: the other six read well in place, cards[6] and r-ih3gzpr1 already agree, e-l2zcmjow still answers Sicilia DOC on a stem that says unless a smaller DOC applies, and every old string occurs once. Grillo as a cross of Catarratto and Zibibbo stands. Completeness: the Nero d'Avola page already says a DOC, most often Sicilia DOC; no other file says Sicilia DOC alone since 2017, and no other place calls Grillo the island's best. Also tested and left: Nero d'Avola as the island's most planted red (still so on the 2021 register figures, see L2-09), and Etna's DOCG, which the record gives as applied for and pending; a report of September 2026 still calls it the next milestone. Left for the owner: the same record's Gulfi line (the grape's best case for terroir) is a superlative of judgement no reviewer flagged.

entriesApplied.topic: Sagrantino's tannin, without a ranking
entriesApplied.claim: The Umbria record says Sagrantino has the highest tannin and polyphenol load measured in any Italian variety and is the most tannic grape in Italy; GRAPES_PLUS says often called Italy's highest and often called the most tannic grape in the world; a producer note says the highest tannin load of any Italian variety.
entriesApplied.finding: No measurement across Italy's varieties was found that ranks Sagrantino first. One study of Sagrantino wines found the highest mean oligomeric procyanidins among the wines it compared, 1.2 g/L against 0.8 g/L for Nebbiolo, a result inside one study's sample. Trade and grape references agree on the substance: small, thick skinned berries and a tannin and polyphenol load that puts it among the most tannic of all grapes.
entriesApplied.why: A ranking needs a measurement to cite and none ranks it first; the substance (among the most tannic of all grapes) stays. Left: ADV a-dq2mo3wg, whose stem asks for Sagrantino's claim to fame, a reputation, so its answer stands; i-70avillq (one of Italy's most tannic) and the CMS's two of Italy's most tannic reds are already hedged.
entriesApplied.refuterNote: The finding says no measurement ranks Sagrantino first across Italy's varieties; one does, within its sample. A survey of 110 single variety wines of eleven Italian red grapes from one vintage (Food Research International, 2021) found Sagrantino highest in total phenolics, 3578 mg/L, and richest in proanthocyanidins and vanillin reactive flavanols, with Corvina lowest at 1065. So the record's measured claim was nearer the truth than the finding allows, but in any Italian variety and the most tannic grape in Italy still reach past eleven grapes and one vintage, and the change stands. The new texts said among the most tannic of all grapes, the very shape of the house rule's own example of a forbidden superlative (most tannic in the world); they now use the comparative the reviewed Sagrantino grape page already uses (more tannin than almost any grape), which both sources bear out. cards[5].b still answers its front (why Sagrantino is famous among grapes). Every old string occurs once; the producer style line sits in a single quoted string, so its new text carries no apostrophe. Should the owner want the measured rank kept, it would need the survey added to the Umbria record's sources: the highest tannin and polyphenol load of eleven Italian reds measured side by side in 2021. Left, and agreed: ADV a-dq2mo3wg, whose stem asks the grape's claim to fame; i-70avillq (one of Italy's most tannic red grapes) and the CMS's two of Italy's most tannic reds, both hedged and both now borne out by the survey. Completeness: Aglianico's and Tannat's GRAPES_PLUS rows compare grip without a rank; no other place ranks Sagrantino.

entriesApplied.topic: Egri Bikavér: at least four varieties, not three
entriesApplied.claim: The Eger record (summary, made.winemaking, law.classification, law.tiers Classicus, exam[0], cards[0].b) and the Hungary country record (exam[1], question r-1ozia0r0) say Egri Bikavér is a blend of at least three varieties, and the country question says the same of Szekszárdi Bikavér.
entriesApplied.finding: The Egri Bikavér product specification that applies to wines marketed from the 2023/2024 wine year asks for at least four varieties, each above 5 per cent of the blend, with Kékfrankos at 30 to 65 per cent and the largest share; the earlier Eger texts asked for more, not fewer (five varieties in the upper tiers of the text applicable from 2012, struck to four in a later draft), and three is the count of older rules (a Szekszárd text of 2009 still wrote three), not of either specification in force. The Szekszárd specification, fourth version, applicable from 15 March 2024, also asks for at least four varieties, with Kékfrankos at 45 per cent or more and Kadarka at 5 per cent or more. The national wine body's own pages and the 2024 Hungarian Wine Summit material give the same: four grapes, Kékfrankos 30 to 65 per cent at Eger. The oak minimums the record gives (six months for Classicus, twelve for Superior and Grand Superior) hold.
entriesApplied.why: Three is the count of a superseded rule: both Bikavér specifications in force ask for four, so every line that teaches three is wrong for the exam and for a guest.
entriesApplied.refuterNote: Tried to refute with the tier rows of the Egri Bikavér specification for the 2023/2024 wine year (search summaries drawn from the ministry registers): Classicus asks at least four varieties, each above 5 per cent, Kékfrankos 30 to 65 per cent and the largest share, eight days on the skins and six months in wood; Superior gives the same Kékfrankos band, with Turán and Bíborkadarka held to 10 per cent between them; Grand Superior again asks four varieties above 5 per cent. Secondary pages that give five varieties or a 50 per cent ceiling for the upper tiers repeat the text applicable from 2012. The second version of the Eger specification is where three varieties and no variety above half come from; versions 3 and 4 (the latter for grapes harvested after 1 August 2017) already ask four. One wrinkle: versions 3 and 4 let an organic Classicus be blended from three varieties; the summaries of the 2023/2024 text show no such clause, so four is the rule and the organic allowance is noted as unsettled. Szekszárd: version 4, for wine released from 15 March 2024, asks four varieties, Kékfrankos at 45 per cent or more and Kadarka at 5 per cent or more; version 1 had asked three and 35 per cent, so the country question's three was out of date for both towns. All eight olds occur once in hungary.1.json at the paths named, and each new line reads in place; the Classicus tier, exam line and card stay true of every tier. Completeness: the Szekszárd record (hungary.2.json), the Régionale primer (four, Kékfrankos the largest share), the Certified primer (largest share) and the Advanced answer (four, handled in L3-02) already agree; no other line in js/, the region fragments, the CMS questions, rewrite/categories or the grape fragments gives three (blaufrankisch.json carries the count only in its review notes).

entriesApplied.claim: Question c-98c4i3oo (rewrite/categories/r2_hungary_greece.py) keys the ceiling on any one variety in Egri Bikavér at fifty per cent and says the upper tiers ask for more varieties; the Advanced answer a-ih3g5con says no single variety above 50% and Superior requires five varieties.
entriesApplied.finding: The Egri Bikavér specification for wines marketed from the 2023/2024 wine year lets Kékfrankos run from 30 to 65 per cent and requires it to be the largest share, so the ceiling on any one grape is Kékfrankos's 65 per cent; the national wine body gives the same band. The fifty per cent band and the five variety rule belong to earlier versions of the Eger specification (the 2012 text), and the summaries of the current text read here give four varieties for every tier, while trade summaries still repeat five for Superior: the count of varieties above the base is not settled by what was read, so the lines drop it rather than give a new one.
entriesApplied.why: The keyed fifty per cent is false under the specification in force, which lets Kékfrankos reach 65 per cent: the stem stands, but its key does not, so the keyed option changes and the integrator keeps the pinned id c-98c4i3oo; in a-ih3g5con the keyed grape stays and only the false gloss goes.
entriesApplied.refuterNote: Tested the ceiling against every tier: the summaries of the 2023/2024 text give Kékfrankos 30 to 65 per cent and the largest share for Classicus and for Superior, and four varieties for Grand Superior; the 30 to 50 band and five varieties that a wine glossary still prints for Superior and Grand Superior are the 2012 text. So 65 per cent is the ceiling on any one grape, since every other grape must sit below Kékfrankos, and the stem stays true; only the key moves, from Fifty to Sixty-five per cent, and the integrator keeps c-98c4i3oo pinned. Read the deal: Sixty-five sits apart from Seventy-five and Thirty, and Ten per cent remains a fair distractor although Turán and Bíborkadarka are held to 10 per cent, since the stem asks the cap on any one variety. The new explanation is ASCII, as r2_hungary_greece.py is, and every clause holds (three more varieties beside Kékfrankos; longer ageing at Superior, twelve months against six; a named dűlő at Grand Superior). In a-ih3g5con the keyed grape and the accept list stay, the answer gloss loses only what is false, and the stem (which grape today) still keys Kékfrankos; the old gloss already said four for the base wine, so the record agreed with itself only after this change. Both olds occur once. The generated js/data-questions.js carries the same stem and follows by python3 rewrite/build.py r2_hungary_greece then ship.py.

entriesApplied.topic: Tokaj: dry single vineyard Furmint from about the turn of the century
entriesApplied.claim: The Hungary country record (overview, grapes[0].styles) and the Tokaj record (summary, exam[5]) date dry Furmint from single vineyards, and its class, to the 1990s: in the same decade as the rebuilt estates, since the 1990s, the dry Furmint movement of the 1990s.
entriesApplied.finding: Dry Tokaji was made in the 1990s: the first commercial dry wines of the post communist years came from the new estates in the early 1990s, and dry Furmint had long been made as the base wine for Aszú. The single vineyard dry Furmint that changed Tokaj's view of the style dates from the 2000 vintage, an Úrágya wine made at Mád after a year of poor botrytis. So the 1990s is right for dry Tokaji and wrong for single vineyard dry Furmint of class; about the turn of the century is true of both. The Szent Tamás note (the 2000s) already agrees and stays.
entriesApplied.why: Dry Tokaji is a 1990s story but single vineyard dry Furmint of class is a 2000 vintage one; the turn of the century is true to both and matches the Szent Tamás note.
entriesApplied.refuterNote: Looked for single vineyard dry Furmint before 2000 and found none: every source read puts the first single vineyard dry Tokaji in the 2000 vintage, from Úrágya at Mád; Decanter dates the wider change to the warm, dry 2003 vintage, when many houses launched premium dry wines, and the first commercial dry wines of the post communist years (Disznókő, Hétszőlő) to the early 1990s. About the turn of the century is true to both, and the 1990s in the region record would teach the wrong decade for the single vineyard wines. The four olds occur once each in hungary.1.json at the paths named; the new overview sentence still reads after the early 1990s clause, and the Szent Tamás place note (the 2000s) agrees. Completeness: no other line in js/, the region fragments, the CMS, rewrite/categories or the grape fragments dates single vineyard dry Furmint to the 1990s (the Furmint grape page gives no decade). The Master answer m-kuunvbip says the late 1990s and 2000s, which agrees, but it names living growers in its answer and accept list, which this lane may not touch (see unsettled).

entriesApplied.topic: Tokaji Aszú at the table: 10 to 12 degrees, warmer than the sweet whites row
entriesApplied.claim: The Tokaj record serves Aszú at 10 to 12 degrees Celsius (wines[0].note, exam[6]); the service reference serves sweet whites with Tokaji named at 6 to 8 C (the temperatures row) and Tokaji Aszú with Sauternes at 6 to 8 C (the digestifs row); the Furmint grape page says sweet Aszú colder, as for Sauternes.
entriesApplied.finding: No statement of the Tokaj wine community was found. The Tokaj houses put Aszú at 10 to 12 degrees Celsius (a Mád house's Aszú sheets), 10 to 13 (a Tokaj estate's six puttonyos sheet) and 12 to 14 (an Aszú on the national wine body's fair pages); the national body's Furmint page puts late harvest Furmint at 8 to 10. The serving references put Tokaji colder than its makers but not as cold as 6 to 8: the Swedish monopoly serves Sauternes and Tokaji at 8 to 10, and a serving guide gives Tokaji Aszú 7 to 12. So the record's 10 to 12 is Tokaj's own figure and stands, the 6 to 8 of the two service rows is colder than any source read for Tokaji, and the Furmint page follows the rows. The sweet whites band itself (Sauternes, ice wine, late harvest) is not in question here and stays at 6 to 8.
entriesApplied.why: The Codex disagreed with itself; Tokaj's makers and both serving references put Aszú above 8 degrees, so the region record stands and the two service rows (and the grape page that follows them) give Aszú its own figure, leaving every other temperature row alone.
entriesApplied.refuterNote: Looked for Tokaj makers who serve Aszú as cold as 6 to 8: one house's recent sheets (Aszú 3 and 5 puttonyos, 2016) give 8 degrees Celsius, its 2014 sheet 10 and its 2008 sheet 10 to 12; a Disznókő listing gives 11 to 13. So the makers range from 8 to 14, centred on 10 to 12, and only one recent sheet touches the top of the service rows' 6 to 8. The region record's 10 to 12 stands as the makers' common figure, and the two service rows giving Aszú its own figure is the smallest change that ends the Codex's disagreement with itself; the sweet whites band for Sauternes, ice wine and late harvest stays. Both service olds occur once in js/data-service-ref.js (hand held), and the rows still read: the why column (cold balances the sugar) holds for the band, and the digestif row's pour and pairings are untouched. The service-ref schema fixes the four columns, not the wording. The Furmint page edit was linted in a scratch copy (build-grapes --lint furmint passes), and Aszú about the same sits beside the dry wine's 10 to 13. Completeness: no other row in the service reference, the pairing, floor or cellar files, the CMS or the banks gives Tokaji a temperature; the Tokaj record's dry Furmint note (10 to 12) and exam[6] already agree. The Furmint fragment's review notes still describe the old disagreement; the integrator may refresh them.

entriesApplied.topic: Furmint: botrytis prone, skin thickness dropped
entriesApplied.claim: The Régionale row for Furmint (INTRO_GRAPES) ends Thin-skinned and botrytis-prone; the Tokaj record calls Furmint thin skinned and botrytis prone (grapes[0].styles); the Régionale question i-2zibe7e9 gives thin skins as a clue to Furmint.
entriesApplied.finding: Every source read agrees that Furmint is prone to botrytis, with a loose bunch and late ripening that let the rot in; on the skin they split. A government vine sheet and an importer's glossary call the skin thin and tie the rot to it; two wine references call the skin thick, one of them tying the rot to the thick skin, and no Hungarian variety description was found to settle it. The Furmint grape page already leaves the skin out for this reason. So the skin claim goes and botrytis prone stays.
entriesApplied.why: The sources split on the skin and agree on the rot; a clue or a trap must not rest on a split, so the skin goes everywhere it stands, the stem of i-2zibe7e9 included (its clue was the disputed fact; the stem still keys Furmint alone, and the integrator keeps the pinned id).
entriesApplied.refuterNote: Searched for a Hungarian variety description to settle the skin and found the split wider than the entry says: a Hungarian grape dictionary and a wine glossary call the skin thicker (the dictionary adds that botrytis takes hold more slowly in dry years), a Hungarian tour journal and an importer call it thin, and no ampelographic text was found. Botrytis prone, late ripening and high acid are agreed by all. So the skin goes and the rot stays. All three olds occur once at the paths named. The stem of i-2zibe7e9 still keys Furmint alone (Hárslevelű also rots nobly but is not the mainstay and carries less acid), its options and explanation stay true, and the text stays ASCII; the stem change moves the minted id, so the integrator pins i-2zibe7e9 (it is named by id in .scripts/cms/map/hungary.json and the CMS review notes, and check-ids.py needs it logged). Built in a scratch copy: python3 rewrite/build.py r1_dessert_sweet passes with the new stem. Completeness: no other line in js/, the region fragments, the CMS, rewrite/categories or the grape fragments gives Furmint a skin (the Sémillon lines that say thin skinned are another grape; the rewrite pilot file and js/data-intro.js follow from the module).

entriesApplied.topic: Tannat and Petit Verdot rows: the climate and the acid dials
entriesApplied.claim: The Régionale rows (INTRO_GRAPES) give Tannat climate Warm and acid 3, and Petit Verdot acid 2; TASTE gives Tannat a moderate climate and acid medium plus, and the profiles give Tannat medium to high acid and Petit Verdot medium plus.
entriesApplied.finding: The acid dial runs 1 to 3, and the rows read TASTE's medium plus as 3 for most reds (Pinot Noir, Cabernet Franc, Blaufränkisch, Aglianico, Mencía and Tannat) and as 2 for a few (Cabernet Sauvignon, Zinfandel, Touriga Nacional), so medium plus sits on either side of the line; the sources read put Tannat's acidity at moderately high to high (and one chart at medium) and the profile says medium to high, so Tannat's 3 holds, and Petit Verdot's 2 is a defensible reading of medium plus that no source or profile shows wrong. The climate is another matter: every other grape TASTE calls moderate reads Moderate, Cool to moderate, Moderate to warm or wider in the rows, never Warm alone; Tannat's homes are Madiran under the Atlantic's rain and mild, damp autumns and Uruguay's humid, maritime Canelones, which the Codex's own records describe so, and the grape page's ladder sets them moderate with only Cafayate and Paso Robles warm. So the climate moves to Moderate to warm and both acid dials stay.
entriesApplied.why: Warm alone is the one place the Régionale row parts from TASTE, the grape page and the Codex's own Madiran and Uruguay records; the acid dials read medium plus the way the other rows do and stay, and TASTE is not touched.
entriesApplied.refuterNote: Tested the dials against the shipped data: TASTE (not touched) gives Tannat acid 2 and clim moderate, and its acid 2 (medium plus) reads as 3 in the Régionale rows for Pinot Noir, Cabernet Franc, Blaufränkisch, Aglianico, Mencía and Tannat and as 2 for Cabernet Sauvignon, Zinfandel and Touriga Nacional, so neither acid dial is shown wrong. The climate is: the grape page (tannat.json) puts Madiran, Irouléguy, Canelones and Maldonado on the moderate rung and only Cafayate, northern Uruguay and Paso Robles on the warm one, and Uruguay's humid, maritime climate and Madiran's Atlantic autumns are moderate. Moderate to warm is a value nine rows already use (Merlot among them) and codex53 only prints it, so nothing parses it. The old occurs once in INTRO_GRAPES. The same row's trap, one of the most tannic grapes, is hedged in the form L2-06 accepted for Sagrantino and stays.

entriesApplied.topic: Viognier and Gewürztraminer: ginger is Gewürztraminer's
entriesApplied.claim: The Viognier profile in js/reference.js lists Honeysuckle, violet, jasmine, musk and ginger among its other notes, while the Gewürztraminer profile's confuse line says Viognier is apricot and honeysuckle without the lychee or spice, and the Codex's grape table makes ginger Gewürztraminer's lead note.
entriesApplied.finding: The references read give Viognier apricot, peach, tangerine, honeysuckle, violet and rose, with musk; a grape guide's primary list (tangerine, peach, mango, honeysuckle, rose) and a merchant's guide have no ginger. Ginger does turn up in Viognier, but as a secondary hint: one guide lists it among the layers, and several Condrieu tasting notes give it (spiced ginger on a merchant's page for one Condrieu, a whisper of ginger spice on another, ginger in drinkers' notes on a third). Ginger, with clove and allspice, is what the Codex and the guides give Gewürztraminer as a lead note, and the Gewürztraminer profile's confuse line and the grape table both teach Viognier without that spice. Cutting the two words from the Viognier profile makes the records agree, and the confuse line stays as it is.
entriesApplied.why: Two Codex records pulled apart on one note; the sources make ginger Gewürztraminer's and at most a passing hint in Viognier, so two words leave the Viognier profile and nothing else moves.
entriesApplied.refuterNote: The finding understated ginger in Viognier: a search of Condrieu notes found it on several, as a secondary hint, so ginger is not false of the grape, and the finding now says so. The cut still stands, for the reason the second sommeliers gave: a profile's other notes are what a blind taster steers by, and ginger is the lead note the Codex teaches for Gewürztraminer; the Gewürztraminer confuse line and the grape table (whose Gewürztraminer entry says Viognier has no lychee or ginger) already teach Viognier without it, so one record pulled against two. Softening the confuse line instead would leave the grape table disagreeing. The old occurs once in GRAPES (js/reference.js, hand held), and the line keeps four notes and its rhythm. Completeness: no other Viognier line in js/reference.js, js/data-grapes-plus.js, INTRO_GRAPES, the CMS or the banks names ginger.

entriesApplied.topic: Superlatives of judgement: Naoussa's producers and Touriga Nacional
entriesApplied.claim: The Naoussa record calls the oldest house's Grande Reserve the classic old-school Naoussa on any list (producers[0].why) and another estate's old vine wine the top old-vine bottling (producers[2].why), and calls a third house's Ramnista the modern reference for structured Naoussa (producers[1].why); the Régionale row for Touriga Nacional (INTRO_GRAPES) opens its trap on Portugal's top red.
entriesApplied.finding: Each is a ranking of the Codex's own, which the house rules keep out of the Codex. The facts beside them stand and are kept: the house founded at Naoussa in 1879 and its long aged Grande Reserve in the old style (the record's own wines and places notes describe that style), the estate's old vine bottling, and Touriga Nacional's deep colour, floral lift and firm structure and its place among the Port grapes. Nobody living is named in the new words; the 1879 founder named in the first line is long dead.
entriesApplied.why: The house rule: no superlative of judgement (top, classic on any list); the lines keep their facts and lose the ranking, and the grape row reads signature as the other rows do (Rueda, South Africa, Uruguay).
entriesApplied.refuterNote: The three original olds occur once each and read well in place; the founder of 1879 is long dead and the house of 1997 is named by its house, not its founder. Completeness within the record: the producers list carried a third ranking the entry left, Ramnista as the modern reference for structured Naoussa, a benchmark claim of the same kind as the classic on any list; it is added as a target (the old occurs once) and keeps its fact, a structured Naoussa in the modern style. The record's other words (the classic style of the old houses, much classic Grande Reserve, the reference appellation for Xinomavro) describe a style or the appellation's standing, not a ranking of a producer, and stay. Touriga Nacional: no other line ranks it Portugal's top red (the Douro question's most prized and the Régionale stem generally rated the finest for Port report a reputation and stay). Not added, since no second sommelier flagged them: Dão's Encruzado is Portugal's noblest white and the other judgement words across the L3 records (see unsettled).
